'''''Triglochin maritima''''' is a species of flowering plant in the arrowgrass family [[Juncaginaceae]]. It is found in brackish marshes, freshwater marshes, wet sandy beaches, [[fen]]s, damp [[grassland]] and bogs. It has a [[Circumboreal Region|circumboreal distribution]], occurring throughout the northern Northern Hemisphere. In the [[British Isles]] it is common on the coast, but very rare inland.

==Description==
It is similar to [[marsh arrowgrass]] (''Triglochin palustris'') but has the following differences: it has [[stolons]], is stouter.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key"/> The leaves are fleshy and not furrowed above. It is not very aromatic.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key"/> The [[raceme]] is more dense and like [[sea plantain]]. The flowers are fleshier.<ref name="Marsh-1929">C. Dwight Marsh, A. B. Clawson, and G. C. Roe Jr (1929). ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20180922063538/https://naldc.nal.usda.gov/download/CAT86200107/PDF Arrow grass as a Stock-Poisoning Plant].'' United States Department of Agriculture.</ref> The fruits are oval, 4 mm long, 2 mm wide.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |year=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne & Co|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0 |pages=488}}</ref>

It varies in height from {{cvt|8-30|in|mm|order=flip|round=50}}. It flowers in May to August; flowers are greenish, 3 petalled, edged with purple, {{cvt|1/8|in|mm|0|order=flip}} across, in a long spike.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ct-botanical-society.org/galleries/triglochinmari.html |title=Common Arrow-grass (Triglochin maritima)<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2007-02-17 |archive-date=2007-02-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070204114358/http://www.ct-botanical-society.org/galleries/triglochinmari.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Complete British Wild Flowers">{{cite book |last=Sterry |first=Paul |title=Complete British Wild Flowers |year=2006 |publisher=HarperCollins Publishers Ltd|isbn=978-0-00-781484-8 |pages=188}}</ref> Common names include '''seaside arrowgrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRMA20|taxon=Triglochin maritima|accessdate=15 December 2015}}</ref> '''common arrowgrass''', '''sea arrowgrass''' and '''shore arrowgrass'''.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

It can be an [[Annual plant|annual]] or [[perennial]].<ref name="Wild Flowers of Britain">{{cite book |last=Phillips |first=Roger |title=Wild Flowers of Britain |year=1994 |publisher=Macmillan Reference Books|isbn=0-330-25183-X |pages=52}}</ref>

''Triglochin concinna'' is a synonym of this species.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=222000441|title=Triglochin maritima in Flora of North America|last=|first=|date=|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2018-09-22}}</ref>

This plant is believed to be toxic, as it can produce [[cyanide]]. However, this is usually when the plant is distressed in drought conditions or due to over harvesting, usually by grazing animals. There is a common belief that this species has been known to cause losses in cattle, with green leaves being more toxic than dried material, yet sheep and deer graze on the plant, especially in rural seaside areas. It could be that belief in the plants' toxicity is apocryphal and based on anecdotal evidence.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://gallowaywildfoods.com/sea-arrowgrass-identification-distribution-edibility | title=Sea Arrowgrass – Identification, Distribution, Edibility – Galloway Wild Foods }}</ref><ref name="Marsh-1929" />
